summary:
Djibouti has no statute that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Articles 353 and 354 of the penal code refer vaguely to "good morals" and public morality without naming same-sex relations, and no provision states the position either way. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, nevertheless marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country in its at-a-glance assessment, and authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these articles. The practical position is that such conduct is treated as de facto illegal despite the absence of an express offence.

Public-morality and "obscene acts" provisions are used against people. No reported case law defines the outer limits of Articles 353 and 354, so the exposure of a trans visitor who is visible, or who engages in any same-sex conduct in a public setting, cannot be predicted from the text alone.

There is no legal gender recognition in Djibouti, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. A trans visitor presenting documents that do not match their presentation has no domestic legal route to align them.

Discrimination protection exists in employment only; there is no broader legal prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Complaints can be filed with the police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH), but the US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report records no official violence cases citable and describes a societal pattern of discrimination rather than state persecution.

Status and conduct are treated as taboo. The same report describes pervasive social and religious intolerance, with people fearing family and community shunning on disclosure, and notes that no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated. A visible trans visitor should expect social hostility independent of the legal position, and should not assume that disclosure to family, employers, or community members will be met neutrally.
tangentialFactors:
Djibouti's legal ambiguity places it alongside jurisdictions where same-sex conduct is neither expressly prohibited nor expressly permitted, but where morality clauses supply a discretionary enforcement tool. Outright International's at-a-glance table nonetheless classifies same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country, a framing that does not match the absence of an explicit offence in the penal code.

The US State Department's 2015 Human Rights Report for Djibouti contains limited LGBT-specific content; the remainder of that report addresses general conditions in the country, including suppression of the opposition, harsh prison conditions, female genital mutilation, and trafficking. These are context for overall state capacity and rule-of-law conditions rather than trans-specific findings.

Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board research from 2009 to March 2012 (response to information request DJI104070.E) found documentation on the treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti to be scarce across all consulted sources, relying largely on the US 2010 country report. That baseline indicates how little legal, protection, or support framework existed in that period.
localsOnly:
Residents of Djibouti have employment-only discrimination protection, with no wider statutory prohibition on discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Complaints may be lodged with the police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH), though the 2023 US State Department report cites no cases of official violence.

Legal gender recognition is not available, and LGBTI organisations cannot register as legal entities. Social and religious intolerance is described as pervasive, with disclosure carrying a real risk of family and community shunning, and no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Articles 353 and 354 have been applied to a trans individual specifically is unresolved in the available sources; no case law defining their outer limits is documented. The 2023 US State Department report's statement that no official violence cases are citable is a reporting finding, not a confirmation that none occurred.

Outright International's classification of same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country, despite the absence of an express offence, is not reconciled in the sources; the basis for that at-a-glance marking is not stated. Whether the CNDH has handled any SOGIESC-related complaint is not sourced.
